problem_motivation.content: Refractory high-entropy alloys currently suffer from poor ductility at room temperature despite high strength, limiting their engineering use.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application

problem_motivation.content: Most RHEAs suffer from poor room temperature compressive plasticity, limiting engineering applications.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: most of the reported RHEAs have poor room temperature compressive plasticity, which makes them difficult to process and limits their engineering applications.

problem_motivation.content: The specific alloy studied has high strength but very low ductility (4.5% compression strain) in its initial state.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: The alloy has a room-temperature yield strength of 2035 MPa but only 4.5% compression strain before fracture in Condition (1).

problem_motivation.content: Identifies the need to improve room temperature ductility of a brittle RHEA through microstructure modifications.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: The main goal of the present work was to improve the room temperature ductility of an initially brittle RHEA through microstructure modifications by thermal treatment.

prior_limitation.content: Metastability-engineering approaches fail for inherently brittle RHEAs that fracture without strain localization.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Unfortunately, this method is only applicable to intrinsically ductile RHEAs that show low tensile ductility due to rapid strain localization and necking. It cannot be applied to inherently brittle RHEAs that fracture without strain localization/necking and, often, without any macroscopic strain.

prior_limitation.content: Existing Al-containing RHEAs have limited room temperature ductility due to the brittle ordered B2 matrix.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: these novel two-phase RHEAs have very limited room temperature compressive ductility, which can be explained by the inherent brittleness of the ordered B2 matrix phase

prior_limitation.content: The ductility improvement methods discussed in the literature cannot be applied to Al-containing two-phase RHEAs.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Unfortunately, the approaches for improving ductility discussed above cannot be applied to this class of Al-containing RHEAs.

causal_claim.content: The high strength of Condition (1) leads to a very low fracture strain.
causal_claim.evidence_span: In Condition (1) the alloy had high room temperature (RT) strength (yield stress σ 0.2 = 2032 MPa, true peak stress σ p = 2035 MPa) but showed a true compressive fracture strain ε f of only 4.7%.

mechanism_principle.content: The poor ductility is caused by the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys

mechanism_principle.content: The high hardness of Condition (1) is caused by its fine-scale mixture of hard B2 and decomposed B2 phases.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The highest hardness was found in Condition (1) due to its fine-scale B2 (hard) + BCC decomposed microstructure

mechanism_principle.content: The intermediate hardness of Condition (3) results from discrete B2 precipitates within a BCC matrix, which is coarser than the microstructure in Condition (1).
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Intermediate hardness was observed in Condition (3) due to the presence of discrete B2 precipitates within the continuous BCC matrix, since the scale of the two-phase BCC + B2 microstructure in Condition (3) is substantially coarser than Condition (1).

mechanism_principle.content: The brittle behavior of Condition (1) is attributed to the presence of continuous B2 channels.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The brittle nature of Condition (1) is due to the presence of continuous B2 channels

mechanism_principle.content: The ductility of Condition (2) is attributed to its single-phase BCC nature with small compositional fluctuations.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: whereas Condition (2) is largely a single-phase BCC alloy with a small degree compositional fluctuations, and thus has more ductility.

mechanism_principle.content: Condition (1) is stronger than Condition (3) because the hard B2 phase is continuous in (1) while the soft BCC phase is continuous in (3).
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: However, Condition (1) is stronger (but less ductile) than Condition (3) since the harder B2 phase is continuous in Condition (1) while the softer BCC phase is continuous in Condition (3).

hypothesis_statement.content: The study proposes that tuning the microstructure can improve ductility while maintaining high yield strength.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: The present study focuses on improving the ductility of this alloy by tuning the microstructure, while maintaining its high yield strength.

hypothesis_statement.content: Speculates that strong element bonding in the B2 matrix causes high strength and brittleness in Condition (1).
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: it can be speculated that strong element bonding in the B2 matrix is responsible for high strength (and, unfortunately, brittleness) of Condition (1)

hypothesis_statement.content: Proposes that precipitation strengthening from B2 precipitates and dislocation mobility in BCC matrix likely play a substantial role in Conditions (2) and (3).
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: while in the case of Conditions (2) and (3), precipitation strengthening from B2 precipitates and dislocation mobility in BCC matrix are likely to play a substantial role.

hypothesis_statement.content: Speculates that anomalous strengthening in the B2 phase may occur via cross-slip between competing glide systems and sessile kinks, similar to Ni3Al.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Anomalous strengthening is not observed in binary B2 alloys, since the critical resolved shear stresses between competing systems are so different, and only one slip mechanism is usually observed. However, the unusual compositional complexity of the B2 phase in the present study may enable two or more different slip systems to compete.

evidence_result.content: Condition (2) exhibits extreme ductility with no fracture observed at strains exceeding 60%.
evidence_result.evidence_span: In Condition (2), the alloy was very ductile at room temperature and did not show any evidence of fracture even after a true strain of 60%

evidence_result.content: Condition (3) shows a peak stress of 1772 MPa reached at a true compressive strain of 16.9%.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Condition (3) provided an intermediate room temperature yield stress ( σ 0.2 = 1345 MPa) and showed noticeable hardening, with the average hardening rate of dσ/dε ≈ 1220 MPa, until σ p = 1772 MPa was reached at the peak true compressive strain ε p = 16.9%.

evidence_result.content: At 600 °C, Condition (1) maintains high yield stress but has low plasticity (3.8% fracture strain), while Condition (3) has lower yield stress but higher plasticity (16.2%).
evidence_result.evidence_span: The alloy in Condition (1) exhibited a high yield stress ( σ 0.2 = 1774 MPa) but low compressive plasticity ( ε f = 3.8%), while the yield stress was lower in Condition (3) ( σ 0.2 = 1423 MPa) but the compressive plasticity was substantially higher ( ε f = 16.2%).

constraint.content: Vacuum conditions must be maintained at 10^-6 torr or higher during compression testing.
constraint.evidence_span: Prior to each test, the furnace chamber was evacuated to 10 −6 torr, and this or higher vacuum was maintained during testing.

constraint.content: Atom probe experiments were conducted within a specific temperature range.
constraint.evidence_span: All atom probe experiments were conducted in the temperature range of 40–60K

constraint.content: The voltage evaporation pulsing is constrained to a specific percentage of steady-state voltage.
constraint.evidence_span: pulsing voltage maintained to 20% of the steady-state voltage

constraint.content: The frequency of the pulsing voltage is constrained to 200 kHz.

contradiction.content: The observation of higher yield stress but lower plasticity in Condition (3) at 600 °C compared to 25 °C is unusual and conflicts with typical expectations, prompting further discussion.
contradiction.evidence_span: Condition (3) had a slightly higher yield stress and lower compressive plasticity at 600 °C than at 25 °C. The reasons for this unusual behavior have important implications for the development of this alloy family for high temperature applications

contradiction.content: Notes that the observed yield strength increase at 600 °C for Condition (3) contradicts the general rule that metal strength decreases with temperature.
contradiction.evidence_span: The strength of metals almost always decreases with increasing temperature, and so the observation in the present work that the yield strength is higher at 600 °C than at RT for Condition (3) is unusual.
